message:
I'm redoing our downstairs bathroom floor myself (first time, slightly terrified) and I've got a pile of questions.

The tile shop guy talked really fast so I didn't catch half of it. Could you explain what "lippage" means in tiling, in simple terms? And what's a sensible grout colour for a pale grey porcelain tile if I don't want it looking dirty after a month? My partner also wants to know whether we should do the floor before or after the new toilet goes in, just a quick answer with a reason.

The floor is 2.4 m by 1.8 m. The tiles I like are 30 cm × 60 cm and come in boxes of 8. Everyone online says to add 10% for cuts and breakages. How many boxes do I actually need to buy?

I also need a short, polite message to the neighbours saying there'll be some noise from cutting tiles on Saturday morning, since they've already put up with a skip on the drive for a fortnight. Finally, any three tips for a beginner laying their first floor would be very welcome. I've watched a lot of videos, but they all make it look far easier than it probably is.

Thank you, honestly.
response:
Here's everything, in order.

## What "lippage" means

**Lippage is when one tile edge sits higher than the tile next to it**, so you get a little lip where they meet. You can feel it underfoot, it catches the light, and bad lippage can be a trip hazard.

It's especially likely with long tiles like your 30 × 60 cm ones, because long tiles are often very slightly bowed in the middle. Two ways to avoid it:

- **Use a tile levelling system.** These are cheap plastic clips and wedges that pull neighbouring edges flush while the adhesive sets. They're well worth it for a first-timer.
- **Don't stagger the tiles by half a tile.** If you want a staggered pattern, offset each row by a third of a tile at most. A half-offset lines up the high middle of one tile with the low end of the next.

## Grout colour for pale grey porcelain

Go for a **mid grey, a shade or two darker than the tile**. Names to look for include "mid grey", "silver grey" or "pewter", depending on the brand.

- **Avoid white or very pale grout** on a floor. It's the colour that looks dirty within weeks.
- **Avoid going much darker** unless you want a strong grid effect. Very dark grout can also show pale residue such as limescale and cleaning-product marks.
- **Use a stain-resistant grout** ("flexible, anti-mould, stain-resistant"), or seal a standard grout once it has cured. Either will keep it looking fresh much longer.

Hold a grout sample stick against a tile in your actual bathroom light before deciding.

## Floor before or after the toilet?

**Before.** Tiling the whole floor first means no fiddly cuts around the base of the pan. It also looks neater, and if you ever replace the toilet there won't be an untiled outline underneath. Just check that the soil pipe connection still works with the floor about 1 cm higher.

## How many boxes

- **Floor area:** 2.4 × 1.8 = **4.32 m²**
- **One tile:** 0.3 × 0.6 = 0.18 m², so you need **24 tiles** with no waste
- **Plus 10%:** 26.4, so round up to **27 tiles**
- **Boxes of 8:** 27 ÷ 8 = 3.4, so **4 boxes (32 tiles)**

**Buy 4 boxes.** That leaves about 8 spare tiles beyond what you'll lay, which is a sensible margin for a first job. You will break or miscut a few. Two more points:

- Your room happens to be an exact multiple of the tile size (4 tiles by 6 tiles). Even so, expect cuts at the walls once grout gaps are added, plus cuts around the toilet waste pipe and the doorway.
- Check that all the boxes have the **same batch or shade number** on the label. Keep a couple of spare tiles after the job in case one ever cracks.

## Message to the neighbours

> Hi both,
>
> Just a quick heads-up that I'll be cutting floor tiles on Saturday morning, so there may be some noise from roughly 9 till lunchtime. Sorry about this, especially after you've put up with the skip on the drive for the past fortnight. Thank you for being so patient. It should all be finished soon!
>
> [Your name]

Adjust the times to suit. Sending it a couple of days in advance is a nice touch.

## Three tips for your first floor

1. **Prepare the floor before anything else.** The floor underneath must be flat, solid and clean. On a timber floor, screw down any loose boards and overboard with tile backer board or exterior-grade plywood; tiles on a flexing floor will crack. On concrete, fill any dips and prime it. Most tiling failures come from poor preparation, not poor tiling.
2. **Dry-lay the tiles first and plan where the cuts will go.** Lay a row of tiles without adhesive, with spacers, in both directions. Arrange things so the cut pieces fall at the least visible edges, such as behind the door or along the wall the toilet sits against. Avoid thin slivers in the doorway. Mark guide lines on the floor and start from the line, not from a wall, since walls are rarely straight.
3. **Mix small batches of adhesive and work a small area at a time.** Spread adhesive over only about two or three tiles' worth before laying them. Spread a thin layer on the back of each large tile as well ("back-buttering") so there are no hollow spots. Every few tiles, lift one to check that the adhesive covers most of the back. Clean adhesive off the tile faces and out of the joints as you go. It's a nightmare once it has set.

Also, wear eye protection when cutting, and a mask if you use a wet saw or grinder indoors. Porcelain dust is not good for your lungs.

You're clearly being careful about it, which is most of the battle. Good luck on Saturday.
